comentarios.texto: The commit scan starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). Once mark_committed prunes already-committed offsets, min_offset jumps past any missing offset, so the next pass treats the gap as contiguous and commits beyond it. For example, with offsets 100, 102 and 103 where 101 never arrived, 100 is committed first and then 103. This contradicts the 'highest contiguous offset' docstring and the gap tests. Start at last_committed + 1 when it is known, and only use min_offset for the first commit.

The contiguity scan starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After mark_committed trims all_offsets, min_offset exceeds last_committed + 1 whenever a gap exists, so the gap is skipped on the next cycle. The first cycle stops at the gap and later cycles commit past it, so the 'contiguous' guarantee holds only by timing. Pick one rule and apply it consistently: either start at last_committed + 1 and treat missing offsets as gaps (or Kafka-compacted offsets) deliberately, or start at min_offset every time.

hist.text: get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) (queue_consumer.py:86), and mark_committed prunes offsets <= committed (line 105). So with 100, 102 and 103 the first pass commits 100 and the next pass starts at 102 and commits 103 past the missing 101, which contradicts the 'contiguous' docstring. Kafka delivers a partition in order, though, so a missing offset never arrives later and the only effect is inconsistent stalling.

queue_consumer.py:86 starts at the greater of last_committed + 1 and min_offset, while queue_consumer.py:105 removes committed offsets. Executing the new tracker with completed offsets 100, 102, and 103 confirms successive scans return 100 then 103 without receiving 101, violating the gap-blocking contract tested in tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:351-372.

comentarios.texto: The wait loop breaks as soon as any commit is recorded, but the test then asserts the committed offset is exactly 105. A commit fired by the 1s loop mid-processing can commit a lower offset, so the test is flaky. Wait until the committed value reaches 105 before asserting.

hist.text: The wait loop in test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit (test_results_consumer.py:1861-1867) breaks once total_items == 0 and any commit exists, then asserts == 105 (line 1870). The commit loop first fires 1s after start (queue_consumer.py:275), so a mid-processing commit is only a narrow theoretical race with the mocked processor; this is test tidying.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1864 exits when queues are empty and any commit exists, then line 1870 requires offset 105. The independent one-second commit loop in queue_consumer.py:273-289 can publish a partial offset before processing finishes; empty queues do not guarantee another commit has published the final offset, making the new test timing-dependent.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getClientsWithPermission runs a full policy evaluation (root.evaluatePermission) for every client resource of type Clients. WHY: Listing clients costs one evaluation per client, so a realm with many clients gets a large slowdown. HOW: Evaluate once with all client resources and scopes, or bound or batch the lookup.

hist.text: getClientsWithPermission runs root.evaluatePermission once per Clients-type resource (ClientPermissionsV2.java:138-142, hasGrantedPermission at 274-276). Resources exist only for clients that have specific permissions, and V1 ClientPermissions.getClientsWithPermission uses the same per-resource pattern, so the cost is bounded and not a meaningful regression.

ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 and :276 do evaluate each resource separately, but the claimed listing slowdown is unreachable through existing callers. The only caller is AvailableRoleMappingResource.java:229, whose calling branches require V1 enabled (:71, :108, :145, :184, :217); Profile.java:283-306 prevents enabling V1 alongside V2. The client listing endpoint in ClientsResource.java:120-165 does not call this method.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: retryCount is only incremented when twilio returns a falsy result or an exception is thrown. It is not incremented when `message` is empty or `sendTo` is missing, for example an invalid or missing phone number. WHY: those reminders are re-attempted on every cron run until scheduledDate, which is the behaviour this PR is meant to stop. HOW: Add an else branch to the `if (message?.length && sendTo)` check that increments retryCount.

hist.text: scheduleSMSReminders.ts:158-188 increments retryCount only when twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy or throws. When message is empty or sendTo is missing, the reminder is skipped without incrementing. It is re-evaluated each cron run until its scheduledDate passes and the delete query removes it. No SMS or external call is made in that case, so the only effect is redundant cron work.

In packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleSMSReminders.ts:158–188, an empty message or missing recipient skips scheduling without updating retryCount; increments occur only on a falsy provider result or an exception (lines 178–195). These reminders remain eligible for selection at lines 48–54 and evade the new retry-limit cleanup at lines 38–40, so the PR’s retry tracking leaves this failure path unbounded until scheduledDate.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readInteger and readNext pass it straight to read(int), which allocates `new byte[-1]`. WHY: a malformed or indefinite-length DER signature throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of the IOException that callers expect. HOW: reject negative lengths in read(int) or in the callers by throwing an IOException.

hist.text: ASN1Decoder.readLength returns -1 for 0x80 (ASN1Decoder.java:133-135) and readInteger passes it straight to read(length) (ASN1Decoder.java:71-72), which does new byte[length] (line 170). A DER signature with indefinite length therefore throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException.

ASN1Decoder.java:80-82 adds the consumed header length before calling read(), so readNext does not pass -1 straight through as claimed. AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:128-134 calls readInteger only on those extracted elements; an indefinite-length integer loses its length byte during extraction and fails with IOException, rather than reaching the negative allocation.

comentarios.texto: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented in the CryptoProvider interface as returning the BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the JDK default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN). Callers that rely on the name will get a non-BC provider. Either document the deviation on this override or return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does when it has no BC.

hist.text: getBouncyCastleProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(default).getProvider() (AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:61-66). Its only consumer, BouncyIntegration.loadProvider (common/.../BouncyIntegration.java:33-39), just needs a provider name and would fall back to Security.getProviders()[0] on null anyway; the authz client has no BC, so this fallback is intended.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:61-63 returns the default KeyStore provider, contradicting common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:35. However, common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/util/BouncyIntegration.java:34-39 already permits a non-BC fallback, so the demonstrated issue is documentation accuracy rather than broken behavior.

comentarios.texto: integerToBytes silently truncates r/s values longer than the curve size, so malformed or non-canonical DER signatures are accepted as a different valid-looking value (signature malleability). Reject values that exceed qLength after stripping a single leading sign byte instead of truncating.

hist.text: integerToBytes truncation (AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:151-163) mirrors BC's X9IntegerConverter used by BCECDSACryptoProvider.java:62-63. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is only used on the signing side (core/.../ECDSASignatureSignerContext.java:33) to convert a locally produced signature, so no signature is 'accepted' and malleability is not reachable.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:151-156 unconditionally discards excess high-order bytes, without checking whether they represent actual magnitude or merely sign padding. The conversion invokes this helper for both decoded integers at lines 133-137, allowing oversized values to become different, potentially valid signature components.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `<%- end if %>` on line 6 is not valid Ruby, because `end if` has no condition. WHY: the template will most likely raise a SyntaxError and the embed page will fail to render. HOW: use `<%- end %>`.

hist.text: `<%- end if %>` on its own line (app/views/embed/best.html.erb:6) is compiled by Erubis with the trailing newline, giving `end if\n<next append>`, which Ruby parses as a modifier if whose condition is the next statement; it is valid Ruby and renders. Only stdlib ERB (which appends ';') would fail, and Rails does not use it.

The new template contains a conditionless `<%- end if %>` at app/views/embed/best.html.erb:6; compiling its generated Ruby confirms a SyntaxError. Existing-topic requests reach this template through app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:12–13, so embedded discussions fail to render.

comentarios.texto: The 413 handler now tells the user the maximum size is a hard-coded 10 MB. That number is not the limit the server enforces, which comes from the site settings or the web server config, so the message can be false. Derive the value from the configured setting, or use a message that doesn't state a number.

hist.text: utilities.js:246 now hard-codes 10 MB for the 413 case, matching the limit the PR sets everywhere else: uploads_controller.rb downloads with 10.megabytes and the server now downsizes images above max_image_size_kb instead of rejecting them, and config/nginx.sample.conf:61 ships client_max_body_size 10m. The 413 comes from the web server, so the message matches the shipped configuration. This is the intended design.

The PR replaces the configured value with 10 * 1024 for every HTTP 413 response in app/assets/javascripts/discourse/lib/utilities.js:245-247; config/locales/client.en.yml:1297 displays it as the maximum allowed size. Although config/nginx.sample.conf:61 defaults to 10m, a deployment with a lower web-server limit will reject uploads while this message incorrectly advertises 10 MB.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The cache is assigned unconditionally, so a failed read stores nil in entryPointAssetsCache. WHY: In non-Dev mode a transient manifest read error discards a previously valid cache entry, and the next call has to re-read the manifest. HOW: Only assign the cache when err == nil && result != nil.

The cache is written unconditionally, so when reading the manifest fails, a nil result overwrites the cached assets. In Dev mode a transient read error discards a previously good cache. In non-Dev mode a cold-start failure is stored as nil, so every caller keeps hitting the file read. Only assign entryPointAssetsCache when err == nil and result != nil.

hist.text: webassets.go:45-47 returns the cache early whenever Env != Dev and the cache is non-nil, so in non-Dev mode the load path, and the write at line 69, only runs when the cache is already nil. A valid entry can never be overwritten. In Dev mode the cache is never served, so overwriting it has no effect, and storing nil on a cold failure just retries, which is the pre-existing behaviour.

The unconditional assignment at pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:69-70 already exists in the base commit; this PR adds synchronization. Development mode deliberately bypasses cached values at lines 45-46, and retaining nil after a cold-start failure necessarily requires retrying, so the proposed guard provides no recovery benefit.

comentarios.texto: After a cache miss, every caller takes the exclusive lock and holds it through the whole load (file read and parse). In Dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed, so every request now serializes behind a global mutex. Do the load outside the exclusive lock, or avoid taking the lock at all when the cache is bypassed in Dev mode. The reviewer did not read the function body (lines 51-68), so the actual lock hold time is unconfirmed.

hist.text: webassets.go:49-50 takes the exclusive Lock and holds it (defer Unlock) through the manifest file read/parse. In Dev mode the cache is never returned, so every call serializes on the global mutex. This only affects development mode, and the operation is a small local file read, so the user impact is negligible.

The new exclusive lock at pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48-49 remains held through manifest loading at line 60, including file opening at line 75 and JSON decoding at line 106. Since development mode bypasses the cache at line 45, concurrent requests using this function, including index rendering at pkg/api/index.go:82, serialize their entire manifest loads.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission iterates every group resource and runs a full permission evaluation for each one. WHY: it is called on every user search and user count for non-global viewers, so the cost grows as O(groups) policy evaluations per request. HOW: evaluate permissions once for the scopes across the Groups resource type and collect the matching resources, or cache the result per request.

hist.text: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission runs hasPermission per Groups-type resource (GroupPermissionsV2.java:121-125), but V2 resources exist only for groups referenced by permissions and V1 GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (GroupPermissions.java:313-317) has the same per-resource loop, so this is an optimisation, not a regression.

GroupPermissionsV2.java:121-125 scans every Groups resource and calls hasPermission, which invokes a separate policy evaluation at line 152. MgmtPermissions.java:351 creates each evaluator independently, and IterablePermissionEvaluator.java:59 allocates a fresh decision cache, preventing reuse across groups. UsersResource.java:398 and :448 invoke this work for counts and searches, introducing a meaningful performance problem as configured group resources grow.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: When immediateDelete is true the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting or flagging the WorkflowReminder row. WHY: Reminders of rescheduled bookings, deleted workflows and deleted steps stay in the DB as scheduled=true with a referenceId, leaving orphan rows. In the reschedule case they stay attached to the old booking. HOW: Delete the reminder row (prisma.workflowReminder.delete) after the successful cancel request in the immediateDelete branch.

With immediateDelete=true, the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row. Callers that used to delete the row (reschedule, workflow delete, step delete) no longer do, and the cron only deletes rows with cancelled=true. The reminder rows are therefore left in the database permanently. Delete the DB row after the cancel request succeeds.

The immediateDelete branch cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row. Callers used to delete the row themselves, and the PR removed that code, so the reschedule path in handleNewBooking now leaves an orphaned reminder row. Delete the row after the cancel request in this branch.

With immediateDelete=true, the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row or setting cancelled. The handleNewBooking reschedule caller expects the reminder to be removed, as deleteScheduledSMSReminder does, so email reminder rows of the original booking stay behind with cancelled=null. Delete the row after the successful cancel request.

hist.text: In the immediateDelete branch, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only POSTs the SendGrid cancel and returns (emailReminderManager.ts:213-223), without deleting the row or setting cancelled. The new reschedule path (handleNewBooking.ts:965-969) uses it, so the original booking's WorkflowReminder rows stay scheduled=true with cancelled=null, and the cron only cleans cancelled=true rows (scheduleEmailReminders.ts:43-51). The workflow and step deletes are covered by the onDelete Cascade on workflowStep (schema.prisma:643).

The immediate branch does return without updating the row (packages/features/ee/workflows/lib/reminders/emailReminderManager.ts:213-222), but the claimed permanent orphaning is false: the cron deletes expired email reminders regardless of cancelled status (packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:34-40). Workflow and step deletion also cascade to reminders (packages/prisma/schema.prisma:587,643), while rescheduling merely retains the cancelled batch's row until its scheduled date passes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the redirect-walk limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment documenting the limit was removed. WHY: trees deeper than 1000 stop resolving to the correct set root, so segments may be split or joined incorrectly. This change is unrelated to span eviction. HOW: restore the 10000 limit unless the reduction is intentional.

hist.text: add-buffer.lua:30 does lower the redirect-walk loop from 10000 to 1000 and drops the comment. This is part of the PR's insertion-cost optimisation: the same script now caps each set at 1000 spans with zpopmin (lines 62-64). Bounding the per-insert redirect walk is a deliberate tradeoff for pathological traces, not an accidental change.

src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 reduces traversal from 10,001 to 1,001 iterations, then uses the potentially intermediate node as the destination at line 45. Descendant-first arrivals across batches can build longer redirect chains; eviction at lines 62–63 removes payloads without shortening those chains, allowing subsequent spans to form a separate segment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the rewritten loadUsers dropped the `organization: { select: { slug } }` selection for dynamic-user bookings. WHY: downstream code that reads `user.organization` for these users now gets undefined, a regression in the query result. HOW: restore the organization select.

hist.text: The rewritten loadUsers (handleNewBooking.ts:731-739) did drop the organization { slug } select for dynamic users. However, nothing in handleNewBooking reads user.organization: the only mentions are the hosts select (line 321) and the IsFixedAwareUser type (line 355), and the code uses organizationId from userSelect. So no downstream behaviour changes.

The organization selection was removed at packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:735–739, but the claimed downstream dependency on user.organization does not exist in this booking path. Organization handling uses organizationId, retained by packages/prisma/selects/user.ts:48; packages/lib/server/getBookerUrl.ts:4–6 uses that ID to fetch branding separately.

comentarios.texto: The number-type test's mock matches on `query.query === 'search-query'`, but the hook sends the search as `substringMatch`, so the mock can never match. As a result, `expect(searchQueryMock).not.toHaveBeenCalled()` passes even if the `type === 'number'` early return is removed. Match on `query.substringMatch` so the assertion can fail when the guard is broken.

hist.text: Fact is right: the mock matches query.query === 'search-query' while the hook sends substringMatch (useGetTraceItemAttributeValues.tsx:53), so the not.toHaveBeenCalled assertion is vacuous. But that matcher is unchanged by this PR: the spec is a rename whose only edits are the hook name and removing the attributeKey prop. So this is a pre-existing test defect.

The matcher at static/app/views/explore/hooks/useGetTraceItemAttributeValues.spec.tsx:120 does use the wrong parameter, but removing the guard would not let the test pass. An unmatched request never resolves its promise (static/app/__mocks__/api.tsx:216-225,237-254), so the await at the test’s line 144 would time out before reaching the assertion.

comentarios.texto: The OAuth `state` is the secret that ties the callback to the pipeline, but it is compared with `!=`, which leaks timing information. Use `constant_time_compare` from django.utils.crypto, and treat a missing state as a mismatch.

hist.text: integration.py:412 compares request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature with a non-constant-time comparison. This is real, but the OAuth state is a per-pipeline CSRF token returned in the URL, so a remote timing attack on it is not practical. Sentry's generic OAuth2 callback (identity/oauth2.py:325) uses the same != check, and a missing state is handled at line 401 by redirecting to authorize.

src/sentry/pipeline/base.py:132-133 computes pipeline.signature solely from the pipeline view names, so the compared value is a public deterministic hash, not the claimed secret. src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:401-408 redirects missing-state requests into authorization without accepting a callback; constant-time comparison would not address the actual state-design weakness.

comentarios.texto: The mismatch test asserts only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. A state mismatch or OAuth failure produces the same text, so the test cannot show that the sender-login comparison is what rejected the request. Assert the pipeline got past the state check, for example by checking that the user endpoint was called and the failure came from the login mismatch.

hist.text: In the new mismatch test, test_integration.py:448-454 only asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. error() (integration.py:132) emits that same default text for a state mismatch, a missing access_token, a missing login and the sender-login mismatch (integration.py:412-433, 500-505). So the test passes even if the rejection does not come from the new sender-login check it was written for.

The state supplied at tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:445 matches the hash computed at src/sentry/pipeline/base.py:132-133, and the mocks at test_integration.py:116-123 provide successful OAuth responses. The test sets sender.login to 'attacker' at line 417 against authenticated 'octocat', reaching the rejection at src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:501-505; sharing an error message does not establish that this test misses its intended behavior.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, and the result of the FlagSqlExpressions check is discarded. WHY: the feature flag has no effect, so SQL expressions stay disabled even when it is enabled, and the inverted `enabled` variable hides that. HOW: if the hard disable is intended, return false with a comment and drop the flag lookup. Otherwise return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

enableSqlExpressions negates the flag into `enabled` and then returns false on both paths, so the computed value is never used. SQL expressions are rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Return the flag's actual value.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Callers that could use SQL expressions with the flag on now always get an error. Return the flag's actual value.

enableSqlExpressions reads as 'is the SQL expressions feature enabled', but the local `enabled` is the negation of the flag and both branches return false. The function is constant-false, so the name and variable misstate the behavior and the flag has no effect. Return the flag value directly, or rename the function and variable to say that SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path. The flag is negated into `enabled`, and the fallthrough also returns false. SQL expressions are therefore rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Return the flag's value directly.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path: the `enabled` variable is inverted and both branches return false. The feature flag therefore has no effect, and every SQL expression query fails to parse with "not implemented". Return the flag's actual value.

hist.text: enableSqlExpressions (pkg/expr/reader.go:194-200) negates the flag into `enabled` and returns false on both branches, so ReadQuery always returns 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' for QueryTypeSQL (reader.go:129-131) even with FlagSqlExpressions on.

pkg/expr/reader.go:194-199 does always return false, causing rejection at reader.go:129-131, but this PR intentionally disables SQL expressions. The same change replaces the SQL backend with unimplemented methods at pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16-21; returning the flag value would therefore expose an unavailable backend rather than restore working SQL expressions.
